name: Madison city
description: Madison already allows ADUs much like the benchmark law, with a few exceptions (its rules are below). In other states, places that already allowed ADUs still saw more permits when a statewide law passed, but they gained less than places that had no ADU rules before. So the law is expected to add fewer permits per 1,000 single-family homes in Madison than in its neighbours.
rights_added_text: None on most single-family parcels. Edge cases only: (1) the reform extends ADUs to single-family parcels in districts where ADUs are not listed (e.g. LMX, MXC, CC, RMX, THV, downtown/urban and employment districts with houses, PD); (2) it removes replacement parking: outside the TOD overlay and the no-minimum districts the principal house keeps its own 1-space minimum (Table 28I-3), so a garage conversion that removes the only space needs a replacement space.
note: Madison follows the observed path of 9 similar cities in Washington and Oregon (0.45 rising to 1.08 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year, 2027–2031) in every scenario, so the law adds less here per 1,000 homes than in its suburbs. This choice will be looked at again in December 2026, when Madison's 2026 permit count is final.

like.title: Cities like Madison
like.text: In Washington and Oregon, 9 cities similar to Madison in size and home values (Spokane, Spokane Valley, Tacoma, Vancouver and Yakima in Washington; Eugene, Gresham, Medford and Salem in Oregon) had a median of 0.45 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year in the first year after their statewide ADU law, rising to 1.08 by year 5. Madison is modelled the same way: with the law, its rate follows that path in every scenario, while every other Wisconsin place, Madison's suburbs included, follows the statewide estimate. This choice is being reviewed.
like.detail: Cities like Madison are defined in docs/gate3/MADISON_LIKE_CITIES.md: 20,000–120,000 single-family homes, median home value $250,000–$500,000, not the state's largest city; the definition was fixed before any city's permits were read. Path, years 1–5 (2027–2031 for Madison): 0.45, 0.54, 0.60, 0.80, 1.08 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year; years 4 and 5 rest on the 4 Oregon cities only, as Washington's law is newer. 6 of the 9 cities also changed their own ADU rules in the same window. The path replaces Madison's statewide-model level (owner decision AQ-042, 2026-10-25); with the statewide-model level instead, Madison would add 191 more permits over 2027–2031 (central scenario). The choice is under review at Gate 5. Why places that already allow ADUs gain less: in the four states with counts before and after their law, the first-year rate after it was about the same however high it was before (California 0.12 before → 0.60 in year 1, Rhode Island 0.23 before → 0.97 in year 1, Washington 0.39 before → 0.68 in year 1, Vermont 0.62 before → 0.67 in year 1; permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year, docs/gate3/POOLED_MODEL.md).

programme.title: Why 2026 is so high so far
programme.text: Of Madison's 42 second homes permitted from 1 January to 23 October 2026, 29 come from one builder's 2025–26 programme of second homes behind existing houses: two-unit detached ADU buildings ("twin home ADU", two homes in one building), single detached ADUs, and additions that turn a house into a duplex, all built to repeated plans of about 998 sq ft per home. Without the programme, 2026 has 13. These are second homes on single-family lots that Madison's October 2025 ordinance allows (up to two ADUs per lot, which may share one detached building). A two-unit ADU building goes beyond the benchmark law, which allows one ADU per lot.
programme.detail: Programme in 2026 to date: 20 permits, 29 homes (9 two-unit ADU buildings = 18 homes, 3 detached ADUs, 8 house-to-duplex additions). Its permits share template specifications: 998 sq ft at $80,000–$90,000, or 2,994 sq ft (3 × 998) at $200,000 for a two-unit building. In 2025 it added 7 of Madison's 14 second homes. The model's current-law rate for Madison uses the complete years 2022–2025 only; 2026 and the programme enter as sensitivity cases (docs/gate2/MADISON_PERMITS.md, section 5b).

name: Pleasant Prairie village
description: Pleasant Prairie, a village in Kenosha County, prohibits ADUs today: its own permit records show 3 second homes on single-family lots in 2014–2025. The law would allow one ADU on every lot with a single-family home, so here it starts from almost nothing.
rights_added_text: Detached and attached ADUs by right in all single-family districts (R-1 to R-6, R-4.5, A-2); repeals the §420-30B dwelling ban for accessory structures.

description: Madison's neighbour, used as a check from the same housing market. It began allowing ADUs in May 2026, so even without the law its permits are expected to rise for a few years. Its records are applications, not issued permits.
